keyPoints: YouTube Music is rolling out a 'Made with AI' label on the player page for tracks 'altered or fully generated' with AI; the main YouTube app follows later.
Partners can disclose AI use as Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI or No Gen AI. Without disclosure, YouTube says it may use 'other signals', including its own detection tools.
The label does not make a track ineligible for monetization, according to TechCrunch. There is no option to block labeled tracks, Ars Technica notes.
Deezer says it will launch a toggle by the end of the year that removes AI-generated tracks, albums and related artists from search results.
Deezer reported in July that over 50% of daily uploads were AI-generated, around 90,000 tracks per day; a survey found about 45% of its users wanted a way to remove AI music.
f1c8e20f7598.context: Streaming services are splitting between disclosure and restriction as AI-generated uploads grow. Bandcamp has banned AI music, Tidal withholds monetization from it, and Spotify tags AI tracks and says it won't recommend 'AI personas'. Apple Music is reportedly preparing its own AI tags.
f1c8e20f7598.whatsNext: Watch for the label's arrival in the main YouTube app, Deezer's filter launching before the end of the year, and Apple Music's reported AI labels.

whatHappened: YouTube began rolling out a 'Made with AI' label in YouTube Music on Oct. 14. It applies to tracks that were 'altered or fully generated' using AI, including cases such as using a generative model to create the composition and vocals. The label appears on the player page, and tapping it opens a menu with more detail about AI's role. Labels will extend to the main YouTube app later.

Partners uploading music can declare AI use under three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI or No Gen AI, according to TechCrunch's reading of YouTube's help page. Tracks that only use pitch correction such as Auto-Tune fall under No Gen AI. Disclosure is optional. If a partner does not disclose, YouTube says it may use 'other signals', and it says it is working with music partners and using its own detection tools.

Ars Technica reports that Google could also rely on SynthID watermarks for tracks made with Google's AI, and on C2PA metadata used by many other AI music tools. Separately, Deezer said it is building a toggle that hides AI-generated tracks, albums and related artists in search results, due before the end of the year.
whyItMatters: The two announcements show the range of responses to AI music. YouTube is choosing disclosure over restriction: TechCrunch notes AI involvement alone does not make a track ineligible for monetization, and YouTube itself offers AI music tools such as Dream Track. Deezer is letting users opt out entirely. Its CEO, Alexis Lanternier, cited user demand, and Deezer pointed to a survey in which about 45% of customers wanted AI music removed.

Ars Technica raises limits on labeling. Many AI tools leave no identifying mark, so a missing label does not prove a track is human-made. And since listeners often are not looking at a screen, a label is easy to miss. There is also no way to block labeled tracks from playlists, which is the gap Deezer's toggle targets.
The scale explains the urgency. Deezer said AI tracks were 10% of daily uploads when it added detection tools last year and more than 50% by July, which puts pressure on larger services to act.
whatToWatch: Key questions are how accurate YouTube's detection proves when creators do not disclose, and whether the company adds user controls beyond labels. Deezer's toggle is expected before year-end, and Variety reported that Apple Music plans to label AI tracks in the same period.

f8c1a7370c13.headline: Google DeepMind uses AlphaProof Code to formally verify key parts of Signal's protocol
f8c1a7370c13.dek: DeepMind's AlphaProof Code agents wrote three million lines of Lean proofs in a four-week project verifying core Signal encryption guarantees, finding no new vulnerabilities; Google won't disclose cost or commercial plans.
keyPoints: DeepMind says AlphaProof Code agents wrote three million lines of Lean proofs to verify the core encryption of the Signal protocol, in a project lasting four weeks.
The analysis found no new vulnerabilities, but flagged known, long-fixed flaws in older Signal versions and showed those versions could not be verified.
The scope was limited: it did not formally verify the entire Signal mobile app, and earlier Signal Foundation verification work gave the team a head start.
DeepMind is releasing the specification and proof; it ran the work free as research and declined to share the cost or say whether a commercial product is planned.
f8c1a7370c13.context: Formal verification uses mathematical proof to show software behaves as specified, and has long been seen as a gold standard in security, but writing the proofs by hand has been slow and costly. AI agents that generate proofs are now making it more feasible, though how well it scales is unproven. Signal's protocol also underpins encryption in Google Messages and WhatsApp.
f8c1a7370c13.whatsNext: Watch whether DeepMind extends AlphaProof Code beyond Signal, publishes cost figures, or turns it into a commercial verification product, none of which Google has committed to.

whatHappened: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to formally verify a number of the cryptographic guarantees of the Signal protocol, using a new framework called AlphaProof Code. DeepMind says the agents wrote three million lines of Lean proofs, and Ars Technica reports the proof-of-concept project took four weeks.

The analysis did not turn up any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the protocol it examined. When researchers ran AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal containing known, long-fixed vulnerabilities, however, it identified them and showed that those versions could not be formally verified.

The scope was limited. The work did not formally verify the entire Signal mobile app, and the researchers acknowledge they had a head start from earlier formal verification work by the Signal Foundation. DeepMind is releasing the specification and proof it developed to support other verification efforts.

DeepMind describes a human-AI collaboration process in which agents contribute and self-correct at almost every phase while humans review at key points. Research scientist Swarat Chaudhuri said the team does not want AI generating both the goals and the proofs.
whyItMatters: Before AI, describing the properties to be proved, translating them into formulas and building the proof was extremely time-consuming. Agents can sharply cut the time spent on the last step, which is what made an analysis like this feasible in weeks. The result also serves as further independent validation of cryptography that protects large volumes of communications on Signal, Google Messages and WhatsApp.

The larger question is scale and cost. Google conducted the analysis free of charge, declined to share what it cost, and declined to say whether it plans a commercial verification product. Pushmeet Kohli, Google Cloud and DeepMind's chief scientist, suggested banks and other firms worried about bugs could one day prove properties of their code. Whether that is affordable remains open, and DeepMind's own researchers say there is a long way to go.
whatToWatch: Key signals will be whether DeepMind applies AlphaProof Code to other software, discloses what such work costs in compute and human review, and whether Google offers it as a product. Independent use of the released Signal specification and proof could also show how reusable the work is.

whatHappened: OpenAI says the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI's consumer product lead for ChatGPT, announced the figure at a press event on Monday, according to The Verge.
